elements.description: A table of rows and columns, drawn from the same column definitions on both sides. Named `data-table` and not `table` because `<table>` is a native html element and vue refuses to redefine one. The two renderers part on what a cell value may be, and they have to: the client one runs before the data is known, so it takes functions for `format`, `href`, `icon` and `params` and resolves routes itself; the server one runs after, so it takes the result already computed in the row — `{label, href}` for a link, `{icon, href}` for an icon. `secondary` greys the header too on the client and only the body on the server, and the refreshing overlay has no server equivalent because a page that is being redrawn is not on screen.

shapes.description: A round, muted icon button for a secondary action sitting in a corner — close, expand, dismiss.
An inline link with an icon beside its label, muted until hovered, for a secondary action inside text or a row.
A round frame at text size holding a portrait, an icon or initials, cropped to fill.
The card: a raised rectangle with a title, a body, media, meta and a footer, each optional.
A conversation — the thread of messages, their authors and dates, and the composer under it.
A row of small things that wraps when it runs out of room: tags, pills, buttons.
Centres its content and caps its width at one of the reading sizes.
Prose written elsewhere — an article, a description, rendered markdown — given spacing, headings and figures.
A file or a directory shown as an icon with its name under it.
The grid that lays disk items out, wrapping at a fixed item width.
A documentation page: sections in two columns, the prose on one side and the code on the other.
The default vertical rhythm between blocks, and `no-flow` to drop it where it is unwanted.
The strip closing a page, aligned on the same gutters as the rest of it.
Every form shape at once, for whoever draws a form and does not want to name them one by one.
The row closing a form, where its buttons sit.
A field whose value is being filled for it, and how it reads while that happens.
What every input and textarea looks like before anything is said about it.
The frame of a form: its groups, their labels, and how they follow one another.
The help text under a field, and the errors that replace it.
A password field and the control revealing what it holds.
A group of radio options, and each option as a row that can be clicked whole.
A native select made to read like the other inputs, caret included.
What a field looks like when it is focused, in error, or refusing input.
Form fields set on a raised ground rather than on the page.
A checkbox drawn as a switch.
The frame a chart is drawn in, filling what it is given and clipping what overflows.
Columns that fit themselves to the room available, or a fixed number when asked.
The horizontal and vertical margins a page keeps at its edges, shared so its parts line up.
The bar at the top of a page: its title, and the controls that belong to it.
The frame of a page — a horizontal or vertical split, and a body that scrolls or does not.
The reset: box model, margins, lists and typographic defaults, applied once to the document.
An introductory paragraph, set apart in italics inside a dashed frame.
An image or a video held at a ratio — square, round, 16:9 — cropped rather than distorted.
A menu, as a bar or as a column: its items, their icons, their counts and their submenus.
A thin line of secondary information between two separators, its groups pushed to either end.
The page itself, and `page--fill` for the part of it sized by the room it is given rather than by what it holds.
A small rounded label for a count, a state or a tag, set in the surrounding text size.
A column with a scrolling track between fixed ends, for a side panel or a toolbar of its own.
Children laid in a row or a column with one gap, optionally split at a point or divided by rules.
The raised ground a block sits on, and the class that tells its children they are on one.
The six tag colours, each as a background and a readable ink, meant to be worn by a pill.
A row of controls above or below what they act on, grouped and separated.
A region of a layout given its own size, splittable, scrollable, and never handing that size to its children.
